narrative:
The model determined that you have a 72.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in your third year of law school, your undergraduate GPA, and your first-year law school performance. All three pushed the prediction toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year class ranking was the strongest influence. Placing in the fourth decile (compared to an average of nearly sixth decile among accepted students) signaled that your performance had not reached the level the model associates with passing the bar. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, added further concern about your academic foundation. Finally, your first-year ranking in the fifth decile (versus a sixth-decile average for accepted students) reinforced the pattern of performance that the model links to higher risk of failing the bar.

Although your LSAT score, family income, full-time status, gender, and race were considered, none of them drove the outcome as strongly as these academic indicators.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your study habits and academic performance now. Raising your grades in remaining coursework, seeking targeted bar-prep support, or retaking the LSAT if feasible could meaningfully shift your profile for future applications. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about how to best demonstrate growth in these areas.
